claims: Lightning occurs typically during thunderstorms.
Lightning occurs during volcanic eruptions.
Lightning occurs during intense forest fires.
Lightning occurs during nuclear explosions.
Lightning produces a bright flash of light (visible radiation).
Lightning produces thunder (the sound of the air rapidly expanding).
Lightning strikes Earth roughly 44 (± 5) times per second.
Lightning totals nearly 1.4 billion flashes annually.
The air around a lightning bolt can reach temperatures of up to 30,000°C (54,000°F).
30,000°C is five times hotter than the surface of the sun.
The return stroke (the bright flash) travels at about 100,000 km/s.
100,000 km/s is roughly one-third the speed of light.
An average bolt carries about 30,000 amperes (30 kA) of current.
An average bolt transfers 15 coulombs of charge.
Megaflashes travel over 100 km (62 miles) horizontally.
A record-breaking flash in 2017 stretched 829 km (515 miles) across Texas and Kansas.
Intra-cloud (IC) lightning is the most common type.
Intra-cloud (IC) lightning occurs within a single thundercloud.
Cloud-to-cloud (CC) lightning consists of discharges between two different clouds.
Cloud-to-ground (CG) lightning is a discharge between a cloud and the ground.
Cloud-to-ground (CG) lightning is the most dangerous type.
Lightning forms when warm, moist air mixes with colder air, creating atmospheric disturbances that polarize the air.
Rapidly rising and falling air inside a storm causes water droplets and ice particles to collide, leading to charge separation.
Charge separation typically creates a negative charge at the base of the cloud.
Charge separation typically creates a positive charge at the top of the cloud.
A stepped leader of negative charge descends from the cloud in a zigzagging, invisible path.
As the negative leader nears the ground, positive charges from the ground reach up, usually from tall, conductive objects.
When the leader and streamer meet, a powerful electric current flows, creating the brilliant, visible flash.
Lightning often strikes outside the rain area.
Lightning strikes as far as 10 miles (16 km) from the thunderstorm.
The National Weather Service advises, "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!".
Substantial buildings with plumbing/wiring are considered safe.
Fully enclosed metal-topped vehicles are considered safe.
Sheds are not considered safe.
Picnic shelters are not considered safe.
90% of people struck by lightning survive.
Sheet lightning is a cloud illuminated from within, with the bolt itself hidden.
Heat lightning is a distant flash seen on a hot night, with no audible thunder.
Ball lightning is often described as a floating sphere of light.
Sprites and jets are Transient Luminous Events occurring high above thunderstorms, such as red sprites, blue jets, and elves.
